clue.text: Second pain, possible result of using needle?

blocks.note: to second a motion is to back it
a sharp pain in the side, as after running

explanation.surface: Someone sewing jabs themselves and suffers a second stab of pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a noun of time or a runner-up; here it is the verb meaning support.
explanation.definitionFit: A backstitch is a common hand-sewing stitch, so it is one thing working with a needle can produce.

clue.text: Polish expert

blocks.note: the verb: to rub a surface until it shines
an enthusiast who knows a subject well, as in a film or history ...

explanation.walkthrough: The capital P tempts you towards the nationality, but it is only there because it opens the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are ordinary synonyms: buffing is rubbing to a shine, and a buff is a keen, knowledgeable fan of some subject.

clue.text: Fellow student unfortunately came last, son claimed

indicators.note: things that go unfortunately go wrong, so the following words come out in the wrong order
what is claimed is taken in and held, so the jumbled words take in the son

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A student has a bad day: they finished bottom of the class, and their son said so.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled CAMELAST becomes CLAS-MATE, and the S for son drops into the middle to make CLASSMATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A classmate is someone taught in the same school group as you, so a peer and fellow pupil.

clue.text: Fine, very steep

blocks.note: of cloth: thin and see-through, like gauzy stockings
of a cliff: dropping almost vertically

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' reads as 'all right', as if agreeing to something; it is the fineness of thin cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dictionary senses: sheer fabric is delicate and transparent, and a sheer drop is perpendicular.

clue.text: Person not appreciating another carving of granite

indicators.note: carving reshapes the stone, so the letters of the rock are cut into a new form

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A sculptor's work in granite is dismissed by someone who does not appreciate it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another carving' hints at sculpture, but 'another' belongs to the definition: the ungrateful person fails to appreciate another person.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrate is an ungrateful person, one who fails to show thanks for what others do.

clue.text: Gather there’s little room after turning round in bed

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so the little room is written backwards
the little room sits inside the word for bed

blocks.note: a cell is a small room, as in a prison or monastery
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Someone lying in bed turns over and finds there is little space left.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed cell goes inside the bed, which splits CO…T around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To collect things is to bring them together into one place, a plain synonym of gather.

clue.text: US state that usually is backed, to some extent

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, so the letters lie within the words 'that usually'
something backed moves in reverse, so the letters read from right to left

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A vague claim about what a US state usually does, hedged with 'to some extent'.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'tHAT Usually' backwards to find the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah is one of the fifty American states, in the west, with Salt Lake City as capital.

clue.text: Crime in newspaper?

blocks.note: the paper is always named with its article, so the first piece is that article
the Financial Times, a British daily printed on pink paper, known by its initials

explanation.walkthrough: Call the Financial Times 'the FT' and you have the crime. The question mark flags the loose wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Theft is stealing, one of the commonest offences in law, so it is a plain example of a crime.

clue.text: Flip out, as might popped cork?

blocks.note: to lose your temper in a sudden rage
read literally: a cork shot from a bottle flies up and strikes the ceiling

explanation.surface: A cork flies out of a bottle with alarming force.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for losing your temper is taken literally for the second definition, which the question mark flags.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to explode with sudden anger; literally a flying cork strikes the ceiling above.

clue.text: Flash gift, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: we are told to go by what is heard, so a word for gift is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: a flair is a natural talent

explanation.surface: A flashy present, or a gift for showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' looks like the British adjective for showy; it is the sudden burst of light.
explanation.definitionFit: A flare is a sudden bright burst of light or a signal rocket, so a synonym of the noun.

clue.text: Furious scoter glad, having knocked out a warbler

indicators.note: knocking something out removes it, so the letter 'a' comes out of the two birds' words
something furious is wild and disordered, so the remaining letters are thrown about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters before one is removed
the letter taken out of the fodder

explanation.surface: An angry sea duck, a scoter, is pleased to have beaten a smaller bird in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' does double duty: it is removed from the fodder, yet the definition also reads 'a warbler'. Take one A out of SCOTER GLAD and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The goldcrest is Europe's tiniest songbird, traditionally grouped with the Old World warblers.

clue.text: Artist, name inspiring witch

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the name draws the witch inside it

blocks.note: to name someone is to call them something
an ugly old woman, a traditional word for a witch

explanation.surface: A painter names the witch who inspired a work.
explanation.walkthrough: Marc Chagall was the Russian-French painter of floating lovers and fiddlers; 'inspiring' is read as breathing in.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc Chagall was a twentieth-century painter and stained-glass maker, so he is a famous artist.

clue.text: Top genius riding the waves?

blocks.note: to surf is to ride waves on a board
an ace is an expert, someone brilliant at something

explanation.surface: A brilliant surfer at the top of their game out on the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like an adjective praising the genius; it is the noun. The genius goes after the surfing because it rides on the waves.
explanation.definitionFit: The surface of something is its uppermost or outer layer, so it is the top.

clue.text: Character with a ticklish sensation

blocks.note: taken as it stands
an itch is a tickling urge to scratch

explanation.surface: A person who is irritating, or someone with a tickle they cannot scratch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person; here it is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Aitch is the spelt-out name of the letter H, and letters are written characters.

clue.text: Socialist dumped flier

blocks.note: something dumped has been left behind
a winger is something with wings, fancifully a flier, and also a fast sports player out wide

explanation.surface: A socialist jilted by a pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot or bird, but WINGER is a sports player who flies down the wing.
explanation.definitionFit: A left-winger holds politics on the left, and socialists sit on that side of the spectrum.

clue.text: Person who’s left relationship with large case

blocks.note: a former partner
ample means plentiful or big

explanation.surface: Someone walks out of a relationship carrying a big suitcase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large case' reads as luggage, but the definition is 'case' alone, in the sense 'an instance'.
explanation.definitionFit: A case in point is an instance or illustration, and an example is exactly that.

clue.text: Vacated pub into which brought different fragrant plant

indicators.note: a vacated building has been emptied, so only the outside letters of the word stay
something brought into the emptied pub goes between its two remaining letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
other means different, as in 'some other day'

explanation.surface: An empty pub is filled with a different scented plant to freshen it up.
explanation.walkthrough: The emptied pub leaves P…B, and the word for different fills the gap; the enumeration splits it as POT HERB.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot herb is a plant grown for cooking, many of them aromatic, such as thyme or basil.

clue.text: Kitchen device that’s old covered in small amount of food

indicators.note: what is covered in something is wrapped by it, so old sits inside the small helping

blocks.note: a taster is a small sample to try
standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An old kitchen gadget caked in crumbs and scraps of food.
explanation.walkthrough: The small amount of food is split as T…ASTER around the old.
explanation.definitionFit: A toaster is the electric appliance that browns slices of bread, found in most homes.

clue.text: Cream in prize vessel tipped over

indicators.note: a vessel tipped over is upside down, and in a down clue that turns the letters end to end

blocks.note: a reward is a prize
a pot is a container

explanation.surface: A prize bowl of cream gets knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cream' looks like the dairy product in the vessel; it means the best, as in 'the cream of society'.
explanation.definitionFit: Top drawer is an idiom for the highest quality or social class, the elite, just as cream means the best part.

clue.text: Speaker, one sending message

blocks.note: a small loudspeaker that handles the high notes
someone posting short messages on Twitter, now called X

explanation.surface: A public speaker delivering a message to the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaker' suggests a person talking; it is the audio component.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweeter is the small high-frequency unit in a hi-fi, and also anyone posting on Twitter.

clue.text: Fix crack after rathole empties

indicators.note: emptying a word takes out its insides, so only its first and last letters stay
the crack word comes after the emptied word, fixing the order of the two parts

blocks.note: first and last letters only
to crack a problem is to solve it

explanation.surface: Mending a crack after a rat's hole has been cleared out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix' and 'crack' both look like repairs to a wall, but 'crack' is the verb for solving a puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: To resolve a problem is to settle or sort it out, which is one meaning of fix.

clue.text: Song plays when dancing in company

indicators.note: dancing letters move about, so the word 'plays' is rearranged
the rearranged letters are placed inside the abbreviation for company

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
standard abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A band plays a song while people dance together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' reads as the people dancing together; in the wordplay it is just the two-letter abbreviation CO.
explanation.definitionFit: A calypso is a Caribbean style of song from Trinidad, with witty topical lyrics.

clue.text: Warm drink

blocks.note: friendly and sincere in manner, as in a warm welcome to guests
a sweet fruit concentrate diluted with water, or a liqueur

explanation.walkthrough: 'Warm drink' reads as one phrase, like cocoa; split it into an adjective and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dictionary senses: cordial manners are friendly and hearty, and cordial is a sweet syrupy beverage.

clue.text: Publish bunch of lies, initially ignored

indicators.note: the initial letter is ignored, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: from the phrase 'a tissue of lies', a web of falsehoods

explanation.surface: A tabloid prints a pack of lies, glossing over the first one.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'a tissue of lies' supplies TISSUE; ignoring its initial T leaves ISSUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue a book, stamp or statement is to put it out officially, which is to publish it.

clue.text: Bandage bits up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: bits are parts or pieces

explanation.surface: Bandaging up the bits that hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bandage up' reads as one phrasal verb, but 'up' belongs to the wordplay as the reversal signal in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To strap an injured limb is to bind it firmly with a band of material, as a bandage does.

clue.text: Forward — is one out?

blocks.note: in football, the attacking player whose job is to score
a worker who has walked out in an industrial dispute is out on strike

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about whether a forward has been sent off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' suggests being dismissed at cricket; the question mark flags the union sense, 'all out' on strike.
explanation.definitionFit: In football the striker is the main attacking player; and a worker on strike is out, withdrawing labour.

clue.text: Curry in the morning, right, fine to serve up?

indicators.note: served up in a down clue means brought upwards, so the letters read from the bottom

blocks.note: ante meridiem, before noon
standard abbreviation for right
OK means all right or fine

explanation.surface: Asking whether it is all right to serve curry for breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: AM, R and OK are written in clue order, then the whole string is read from the bottom of the light.
explanation.definitionFit: A korma is a mild, creamy dish of Indian cooking, one type of curry.

clue.text: Classic dealings curtailed

indicators.note: curtailed literally means with the tail cut off, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: trade is commercial dealing

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned business dealings are cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: Trad is a British informal shortening, best known from trad jazz, the revived New Orleans style.
explanation.definitionFit: Trad is short for traditional, as in trad jazz, so it describes something classic or old-style.

clue.text: General item in biscuit tin?

blocks.note: the Italian soldier who led the redshirts in unifying Italy in the 1800s
a flat British biscuit with a layer of squashed currants, named after that soldier

explanation.surface: A miscellaneous item found in a tin of biscuits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like an adjective, as in 'a general item'; it is the military rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Garibaldi was a famous Italian military commander, and the currant biscuit bears his surname.

clue.text: Someone in boat, one having an argument?

blocks.note: a person pulling on oars
a quarrel is a row, rhyming with cow, so the question mark allows a jokey noun for someone quarrelling

explanation.surface: A quarrel breaks out among the people in a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The same spelling has two sounds: row as in oars, and row meaning argument; the question mark flags the invented second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An oarsman propels a boat, and fancifully anyone quarrelling noisily could be named the same way.

clue.text: Mature response is particularly effective, initially

indicators.note: initially points to the start of each word, so just the first letter of each is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of four words

explanation.surface: Praise for a grown-up reply that works especially well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mature response' reads as one phrase, but only 'Mature' defines; the rest spells the answer by its first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripe fruit is fully developed and ready, so ripe is a synonym for mature.

clue.text: European team very angry in America, eliminated

blocks.note: in American slang, real means very, as in 'real good'
no letters: it tells you the word for very is the American usage
mad means furious, especially in American usage
to be rid of something is to have got it out of the way

explanation.surface: A European side, livid after being knocked out of a tournament in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In America' qualifies 'very': REAL for very is American usage, as in 'real good'.
explanation.definitionFit: Real Madrid is the famous Spanish football club, one of the most successful sides in European competition.
